directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Ann magnolia blooms later than star magnolia, helping its flowers dodge late spring frosts that damage earlier-flowering magnolias. One of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum for later, frost-dodging bloom, it produces rich reddish-purple, tulip-shaped flowers on a compact, shrubby, multi-stemmed plant well suited to smaller gardens where full-sized magnolia trees would be too large. Its later flowering window, roughly two to four weeks after star magnolia, gives it a significant advantage over earlier magnolias in regions with unpredictable late frosts, which often blacken and ruin the flowers of earlier-blooming cultivars. Water regularly during establishment and dry spells, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune minimally, since magnolias generally need little pruning beyond removing damaged or crossing branches.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Elizabeth magnolia was the first yellow-flowered magnolia hybrid widely introduced to the nursery trade. Bred at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden and released in the 1970s, this landmark hybrid was the first widely available magnolia with soft, primrose-yellow flowers, a color previously unseen in cultivated magnolias, opening on bare branches in early to mid spring before the leaves emerge, with a light, sweet lemon fragrance. Its introduction opened the door to the many yellow-flowered magnolia hybrids bred since, and it remains a garden favorite for its unusual color, upright pyramidal form, and good resistance to the late-frost damage that plagues some earlier-blooming white magnolias. Water regularly during establishment, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune minimally, removing only damaged or crossing branches as needed.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Stellar Pink dogwood is a Rutgers-bred hybrid with strong resistance to dogwood anthracnose and borers, which trouble many flowering dogwoods. A hybrid between the native flowering dogwood and the Asian kousa dogwood developed at Rutgers University, it combines the classic large, showy, soft pink bracts of flowering dogwood with the improved disease and pest resistance of its kousa parent, addressing the anthracnose and borer problems that have devastated many straight Cornus florida plantings in recent decades. Blooming in mid-spring between the earlier flowering dogwood and later kousa dogwood bloom windows, it provides reliable pink flower color on a tough, adaptable small tree well suited to a woodland edge or specimen planting. Water during establishment and dry spells, mulch to keep roots cool, and avoid the anthracnose and borer problems common to straight dogwood species by choosing this resistant hybrid for new plantings.
